claims.claim: Harold Bloom, in the Library of America tribute page, states that in Le Guin every word was exactly in place and every sentence or line had resonance.
claims.source: Harold Bloom, in "Fellow writers remember Ursula K. Le Guin, 1929–2018", Library of America, January 2018
claims.quote: Every word was exactly in place

claims.claim: Amanda Craig states that Earthsea gains the mysterious depths of Tolkien’s world without Tolkien’s back-stories and verse.
claims.source: Amanda Craig, "Classic of the month: A Wizard of Earthsea", The Guardian, 24 September 2003
claims.quote: the mysterious depths of Tolkien’s, but without his tiresome back-stories

claims.claim: Amanda Craig states that A Wizard of Earthsea contains allusions to fragmented legends about the tragedies of heroes and heroines.
claims.source: Amanda Craig, "Classic of the month: A Wizard of Earthsea", The Guardian, 24 September 2003
claims.quote: allusions to fragmented legends about the tragedies of heroes

claims.claim: Jo Walton states that Tehanu reads aloud beautifully, as she found while reading it aloud to a baby.
claims.source: Jo Walton, "A Woman on Gont: Ursula K. Le Guin’s Tehanu", Tor.com/Reactor, 25 October 2011

claims.claim: Jo Walton states that The Tombs of Atuan is beautifully written but, unlike A Wizard of Earthsea, is not told like a legend.
claims.source: Jo Walton, "Let her be eaten: Ursula K. Le Guin’s The Tombs of Atuan", Tor.com/Reactor, 2011
claims.quote: beautifully written, but it isn’t told like a legend

claims.claim: Jo Walton states that The Tombs of Atuan keeps the reader straightforwardly behind Tenar’s shoulder for the whole book.
claims.source: Jo Walton, "Let her be eaten: Ursula K. Le Guin’s The Tombs of Atuan", Tor.com/Reactor, 2011
claims.quote: straightforwardly right behind Tenar’s shoulder the entire time

claims.claim: Jo Walton states that a lesser writer would have ended The Tombs of Atuan with the earthquake and the triumphant escape, and that Le Guin instead carries on into the escape through the mountains.
claims.source: Jo Walton, "Let her be eaten: Ursula K. Le Guin’s The Tombs of Atuan", Tor.com/Reactor, 2011
claims.quote: a lesser writer would have finished the book with the earthquake

claims.claim: Julie Phillips reports that Le Guin learned from Thomas Hardy to handle strong feeling by pouring it into landscape so the setting carries part of the emotional charge.
claims.source: Julie Phillips, "The Fantastic Ursula K. Le Guin", The New Yorker, 17 October 2016
claims.quote: letting the settings carry part of the emotional charge
claims.page: section on her reading as a girl

claims.claim: Le Guin, quoted by Julie Phillips, rejects the term "pathetic fallacy" for letting a landscape carry feeling and calls the technique art.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, in interview with Julie Phillips, The New Yorker, 17 October 2016
claims.quote: It’s not a fallacy; it’s art
claims.page: section on her reading as a girl

claims.claim: Richard D. Erlich states that Tehanu gains a different style from the Earthsea trilogy, which he calls a welcome variation from the high-fantastic.
claims.source: Richard D. Erlich, Coyote’s Song: The Teaching Stories of Ursula K. Le Guin (SFRA digital book, 2009 revision), chapter "Earthsea Revisited: Tehanu"
claims.quote: a welcomed variation from the high-fantastic
claims.page: chapter Earthsea Revisited: Tehanu, closing section

claims.claim: Richard D. Erlich, with a linguist colleague, describes the opening sentence of Always Coming Home as past conditional, semi-conditional and emphatic past perfect, implying futurity.
claims.source: Richard D. Erlich, Coyote’s Song: The Teaching Stories of Ursula K. Le Guin (SFRA digital book, 2009 revision), chapter "Always Coming Home: Future Ethnography", endnote 29

claims.claim: Michael Dirda states that the narrating voice of the first three Earthsea books is that of a chronicler or mythmaker.
claims.source: Michael Dirda, "The Twilight of an Age of Magic" (review of Tehanu), The Washington Post, 25 February 1990
claims.quote: the voice that of the chronicler or mythmaker
claims.page: review body, paragraph on the earlier novels

claims.claim: Michael Dirda characterises the prose of the Earthsea trilogy as grave and elevated, a style of moral seriousness.
claims.source: Michael Dirda, "The Twilight of an Age of Magic" (review of Tehanu), The Washington Post, 25 February 1990
claims.quote: The prose is grave and elevated, a style of moral seriousness
claims.page: review body, paragraph on the earlier novels

claims.claim: Michael Dirda states that Tehanu is consequently meditative, somber, even talky, in contrast to the journeying of the earlier books.
claims.source: Michael Dirda, "The Twilight of an Age of Magic" (review of Tehanu), The Washington Post, 25 February 1990
claims.quote: It is consequently meditative, somber, even talky

claims.claim: Michael Dirda states that Le Guin can still stand your hair on end with her sentences, and introduces a quoted Tehanu passage as the demonstration.
claims.source: Michael Dirda, "The Twilight of an Age of Magic" (review of Tehanu), The Washington Post, 25 February 1990
claims.quote: stand your hair on end with her sentences

verdicts.trueWording: letting the settings carry part of the emotional charge

verdicts.trueWording: It's not a fallacy; it's art
verdicts.note: Same live New Yorker fetch, the sentence immediately after the Hardy sentence: Le Guin, quoted directly, says 'There's a patronizing word for that: the pathetic fallacy,' then 'It's not a fallacy; it's art.' Attribution to Le Guin is explicit ('she says').

verdicts.trueWording: a welcomed variation from the high-fantastic
verdicts.note: Wayback raw id_ capture of sfra.org/Coyote/earthsea.htm (20151107114510), the URL as given; fetched directly, no live-host attempt needed. Closing section of 'Earthsea Revisited: Tehanu', numbered paragraph 53: '...we gain the possibility for a different style than that of the Earthsea trilogy, and, to my tastes, if not a better style, a welcomed variation from the high-fantastic.' Erlich's wording is 'the possibility for a different style' — a hedge the claim drops, though the same sentence does affirm the variation.

Wayback raw id_ capture of sfra.org/Coyote/alwayshome.htm (20151107114510). Endnote 29: the opening sentence of Always Coming Home is 'a self-reflexive artistic sentence' whose tense, aspect and mood are 'past conditional, semi-conditional, emphatic past perfect, implying futurity.' The colleague limb is explicit — 'consultation with Max Morenberg, a linguist in my department, 8 May 1995' — though the note credits a Stephens paper as a co-source, which the claim omits.
